analysis.investment_thesis: Clear Secured Services trades at INR 111 — a 39% premium to my Graham Number of ~INR 80 — with no margin of safety whatsoever. The business generates consistently negative free cash flow while tripling its debt in two years, the precise opposite of what a defensive investor requires.
key_strengths: Revenue growing solidly: 309 → 476 Cr (+54% in two years)
ROCE of 20.4% suggests decent capital deployment efficiency
High promoter holding (73%) aligns management with business continuity
key_risks: Free cash flow deeply negative all three years: -3, -7, -26 Cr — worsening trajectory
Debt nearly tripled: 44 → 128 Cr; Debt/Equity at 0.94x vs my 0.5x ceiling
Net profit fell to 10 Cr in 2025 despite 37% revenue growth — margin deterioration
red_flags: Graham Number ~INR 80; current price INR 111 — no margin of safety, stock is overvalued
Interest coverage only 3.1x (31 Cr EBIT / 10 Cr finance cost) — below my 3.5x minimum
Finance costs jumped 2.5x in one year (4 → 10 Cr); company is funding operations with debt
No dividend history — zero cash returned to shareholders
CWIP surged from 1 → 22 Cr; capital-intensive expansion funded entirely by borrowings
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Clear Secured Services fails virtually every quantitative filter I apply. The P/E of 18.8x exceeds my ceiling of 15x; the Price-to-Book of 1.79x (243 Cr market cap / 136 Cr equity) exceeds my 1.5x limit; and the Graham Number of approximately INR 80 — derived from EPS of ~4.57 and book value per share of ~62 — places the stock at a 39% premium to what the arithmetic says it's worth. The debt-to-equity ratio of 0.94x is nearly double my 0.5x maximum, and interest coverage at 3.1x sits below my 3.5x floor.

What troubles me most is the cash flow picture. A business that reported operating cash flow of -2, +1, and -22 Cr over three consecutive years is not generating real earnings — it is consuming capital. Free cash flow of -26 Cr in 2025, financed by 37 Cr of new borrowings, tells me this company is essentially paying its bills with debt. Facility management is an inherently thin-margin, labor-intensive business (net margin of 2.1%), and there is no durable competitive advantage evident in the numbers. Mr. Market is pricing this as a growth story; I see a leveraged services firm with deteriorating profitability and no tangible margin of safety.
